body.text: Revelations of a widespread Indonesian wiretapping scheme in which the President was bugged by his own national police highlights a behind-the-scenes power struggle and raises questions about unchecked police power, write Yohanes Sulaiman.

On November 3, Jakarta was shocked by the news that three senior police generals had been arrested over a massive illegal phone bugging scheme that targeted state officials, politicians, journalists, businesspeople, and mass-organisation and NGO leaders.
Extraordinarily, among those subject to eavesdropping were President Prabowo Subianto and two of his predecessors.

The most prominent of the generals detained was Listyo Sigit Prabowo, former chief of police and currently head of the Presidential Staff Office (KSP). With him were Inspector General Ahrie Sonta Nasution, head of the police legal division, and Inspector General Eko Hadi Santoso, a senior instructor at the police staff college. All three are being held at the National Police detention center.The alleged role of such senior police officials raises the question of possible motives and the implications for Indonesian politics, at least in the near future. The search for motives must be set against the background of a behind-the-scenes power struggle between former president Joko Widodo (Jokowi) and Prabowo.

The two men competed twice for the presidency, in 2014 and 2019. They joined forces after the 2019 election, when Prabowo became Jokowi's minister of defence. In 2024, Jokowi again joined forces with Prabowo, this time by having his son, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, run as Prabowo's vice-presidential candidate. Still, this was more a marriage of convenience, to further each other's ambitions, than a true political alliance.

The first visible break came in August 2025. Protests in Jakarta escalated after a police tactical vehicle hit and killed Affan Kurniawan, an online delivery motorcycle driver, on August 28. On August 31, Prabowo, flanked by leaders of political parties, tried to bring calm to the situation.

Standing beside him was Megawati Soekarnoputri, whose party, PDI-P, had expelled Jokowi and Gibran eight months earlier. Conspicuously missing were Jokowi himself, Gibran, and Jokowi's younger son, Kaesang Pangarep, chairman of the Indonesian Solidarity Party (PSI). Not surprisingly, many frame Listyo's alleged conduct in this context. With Jokowi out of power and lacking formal means to oppose Prabowo, access to Prabowo's communications would be valuable.To be fair, the investigation has not yet established the purpose of the wiretapping, and any mastermind behind it remains unknown.

The timing of the case, however, is convenient for Prabowo. Gibran has come under heavy flak over whether he ever obtained a high school diploma. In October, the Constitutional Court dismissed a petition to disqualify him because the petitioners lacked standing, though it said it found no convincing evidence that he held a foreign high-school-equivalent diploma. On October 30, according to the petitioner, the Supreme Court annulled the equivalency certificate he used to register for the 2024 election, prompting calls for his resignation.

Prabowo also recently reshuffled the police leadership and finally removed Listyo. Former coordinating minister for political, legal and security affairs Mahfud MD noted that it was not Prabowo's first attempt, as he tried at least four times to replace Listyo, and each time the plan stalled. One attempt faded after Jokowi and his wife, Iriana, visited Prabowo's residence in October 2025, and Mahfud said the prevailing reading was that Jokowi objected. After that, Prabowo tried to keep his plans secret.

When the move finally came, it was abrupt. On the morning of October 1, Listyo stood behind Prabowo at an annual commemoration of six Army generals killed in the 1965 coup attempt. That same morning, the parliament received a presidential letter, dated the day before, asking it to dismiss Listyo and approve Suyudi Ario Seto, head of the National Narcotics Agency, as his replacement.

Suyudi was the only candidate. His fit-and-proper test lasted about 30 minutes and ended in approval by acclamation, and Prabowo swore him in that afternoon. Hours later, Listyo also was sworn in as head of the KSP, an office that depends entirely on the president for its power. It is a gilded cage. Shortly before the ceremony, Listyo told reporters he had been told he would head the KSP and hoped “that is not wrong.” Within 24 hours, Suyudi had reshuffled 78 generals and 10 mid-ranking officers.

The investigation of the wiretapping happened by chance. The police say it started on October 30, when an officer reported that the suspects had ordered recordings of phone conversations deleted from the police interception system earlier that month. Suyudi briefed Prabowo before the suspects were named, and the president asked for firm legal action. In a later statement, Prabowo said the actions “bordered on treason”. Ahrie's lawyer says his client, a former aide to both Listyo and Prabowo, only analysed numbers handed to him by his superiors and other police units, and denies tapping anyone in the palace.

Whatever the investigation finds about motive, the case serves Prabowo's consolidation of the police. Since October 1, Suyudi has carried out five major rounds of transfers. The latest, signed on November 2, the day before the suspects were named, moved 264 officers, from district police chiefs to deputy provincial chiefs.

The investigation also remains open. Yusril said more suspects are possible, and a fourth general is still being questioned as a witness. Officers who rose under Listyo now have good reason to keep their heads down. Adrianus Meliala, a former member of the National Police Commission, suspects that the wiretapping served "not the state or the police, but the interests of another party." In his view, the police under Listyo played politics, and "whoever plays politics must be ready for the political consequences."

The military has also moved. On November 4, the armed forces confirmed that about 20,000 marines were being deployed to Jakarta. A spokesman called it a routine readiness measure and denied any link to current cases. According to a letter reported by the media, however, the first units began moving on November 2, a day before the suspects were named.

The larger problem is likely to outlast this contest. The police say the suspects entered numbers into the interception system without verification for as long as two years, and nobody stopped them until an officer reported the deletion. Under police rules, a wiretap requires a court's permission and can last no more than 30 days without renewed authority. The police inspectorate calls the case the work of rogue individuals, not institutional policy.

The system that allowed a police chief to listen to the president, journalists, and NGO activists now sits under his successor. Prosecuting Listyo punishes one misuse of that system, but it does not change who can use it next.
Without independent oversight of police interception, the same capacity remains available to whoever controls the police, whether the target is a president or his critics.
